Introduction
This is the fifth episode in an eight-part series.
In the previous two episodes, we looked at the Alan Bradley PLC2 and the Siemens S5 series of PLCs.
In those episodes, we mentioned IOModules, but didn't really go into any detail on them.
Instead, we looked at the CPU units and focused on things from the programmer's perspective.
In this episode, we will look at the I.O. modules, what they are, how they work, and the purpose that they serve in the system.
In addition to this, I will discuss machine safety systems, and also claims made by certain people about cybersecurity and industrial safety.
What is I.O.? First though, we must address the question of what I.O. is.
While the CPU module may run the program, in order for the program to do anything useful,
it must interact with the real world outside the PLC.
It must sense the state of the machine it is controlling through inputs, and it must affect
the operation of the machine through outputs.
A simple example.
Let's take a very simple example to try to make the above a bit more tangible.
assuming we wish to press two parts together, such as pressing a bearing into a housing.
This is a very common industrial process.
Let us assume we have the following items which connect to the inputs.
An emergency stop circuit, a safety system to protect the operator, a part present sensor
used to detect that the housing was correctly placed in the tooling, another part present
sensor used to detect that the bearing was correctly placed in the tooling.
A sensor which indicates the hydraulic cylinder is fully retracted, another sensor which indicates
the hydraulic cylinder is fully extended and the part was fully pressed home, a button
which the operator uses to initiate the press cycle, another button which the operator can
use to abort the press cycle in the event of a fault.
We also have the following items which connect to the outputs, a hydraulic valve with two
solenoids down and up, a pilot light which tells the operator that the cycle was completed
successfully and the part is good, a pilot light which tells the operator that the cycle
was not completed successfully and the part is bad.
This gives us a total of 8 inputs and 4 outputs.
A typical, very small PLC would be suitable for this application.
The PLC program would look at the state of the inputs and apply the necessary logic to
turn the outputs on or off at the appropriate time.
As you can see, what makes the PLC useful is its ability to control I.O.
Small PLCs typically have a limited amount of I.O. built into the same package as the CPU
and can be used as is right out of the box.
Medium to large PLCs will interface to racks of IO,
and the number of IO points can be in the dozens
to hundreds and even the thousands.
Types of IO, the above example is very simple.
There are in fact many types of IO.
I will outline the most common ones here.
The first is digital IO.
This is overwhelmingly the most common type.
Digital I.O. are basic on-off signals.
A digital input will detect if a switch is on or off.
A digital output will turn a relay or valve on or off.
Digital I.O. comes in three main types,
categorized by the type of electronic device used.
These are AC, relay, and DC.
ACIO was the earliest type but is largely faded away by now.
This works with 100 to 120 volts AC.
or 230 volts AC.
Inputs detect the presence or absence of these voltages
and outputs output these voltages when turned on.
The relay logic that the PLCs replaced was largely driven
by these voltages so being able to interface
with existing systems was an important design consideration
for early PLCs.
Relay outputs were an alternative to the tri-act devices used for solid-state AC outputs.
These were very small relays built into the output modules.
Their main attraction was they were usually somewhat cheaper than solid-state outputs.
However, they suffered from being much less durable and had a shorter life.
By the 1980s and 90s AC and relay IO had been largely replaced in new applications by
24 volts DC.
This allowed for more compact and less expensive control wiring and fewer electrical safety
concerns.
Both inputs and outputs worked with 24 volts DC.
All of the standard sensors, solenoid valves, relays, push buttons, lights and pretty much
all other devices were designed to be compatible with 24 volts DC.
In cases where you had a large motor contact or relay or large solenoid valves
which required higher voltages for practical reasons,
an additional interposing relay could be used to amplify the control signal.
IOModules or cards came in 8, 16, and 32 point sizes,
and there are modules which combine both inputs and outputs in a single module.
Analog I.O.
As well as simple on-off voltages, PLCs could also work with variable voltages where the actual
voltage or current represents a measurable value such as temperature or dimension.
These are known as analog values.
These could be inputs or outputs and are known as analog inputs or analog outputs.
The simplest is voltage.
The most common standard voltage ranges are 0 to 10 volts plus or minus 10 volts 0 to 5
volts 1 to 5 volts.
Another type is current.
This is where the amount of current rather than the level of the voltage is what is significant.
Current has an advantage over voltage in that it is less affected by resistance losses
in long wiring runs and is also less prone to being influenced by electrical noise due
to the lower impedance.
The most common standard current ranges are 4 to 20 milliamps and 0 to 20 milliamps.
Another common type is thermocouple inputs.
These have special circuitry built into them to interface with thermocouple devices, which
are a common device used to measure temperature by measuring the voltage generated when two
dissimilar metals are heated in contact with each other.
Serial communications A number of PLCs have serial communications ports, mainly used to
interface with things like label printers or barcode readers.
Some of these even have basic interpreters built into them, mainly to allow for better string
formatting or parsing.
Another category of IO are Servo and Stepper Motor Controllers.
Another type are Counter Timer Modules, which allow for high-speed counting of events, or
very precise timing of events in hardware, or interfacing with rotary or linear encoders.
are measuring devices which have a series of very small but precise marks which interrupt
beams of light when they move, allowing measurements to be made.
Many PLCs also support some sort of networking. I won't go into any detail on that here,
but will instead address this area in another episode. However, network ports may be built
into the CPU or may reside in separate network I-O modules.
As well as the preceding, there are many other specialty modules which you won't bother
to describe here.
Operator Panels The original operator panels were arrays
of push buttons, pilot lights, and other basic operator controls mounted in boxes for an operator
to interact with the machine.
on these were replaced by special.
Virtual-T electronic devices which were also known as operator panels as they serve the
same function.
Modern operator panels are screens and keypads which are used to display information to an
operator or to allow data to be entered into the PLC.
While not strictly speaking a type of I.O., operator panels typically look like I.O. to
the PLC CPU.
on a touchscreen may be effectively the same thing as actual hardware buttons from the PLC's
perspective, and analog values output to the operator panel for display are like hardware
analog devices. All of these data are mapped to memory locations in the PLC with the details
of how this is done varying according to the make and model of PLC.
I won't go into any detail on this, as this could be a separate subject on its own.
Generally though, you would use software to create screens to display on the operator panel.
The indicators and buttons defined in your screens would be mapped to addresses in the
PLC, either directly or indirectly.
This configuration would then be downloaded into the operator panel.
Your PLC program could then interact with the operator panel using ordinary ladder logic.
Safety Systems Up to now I have mentioned only PLCs in any detail.
There is however more to a complete machine control system than just a PLC.
One of these is safety systems.
I will leave out historical safety systems and just focus on modern ones.
I will also leave out large process industries involving things like boilers or chemical reactors
and just focus on assembly operations in industries such as automobiles, appliances and other similar
things.
This won't be a tutorial on safety design, just a very brief overview.
An industrial machine must be designed with safety as one of its fundamental design principles.
If the machine cannot be operated safely, then it cannot be put into use.
Safety must take into account the operators, bystanders, and maintainers.
You must assume that people will be inattentive or make mistakes.
You must also assume that the PLC program will have bugs and the electronics will fail
in a state which could cause a hazard if it is permitted to.
In other words, the PLC and your PLC program are not part of the safety system.
The safety system will decide when the PLC will be permitted to act and when it will not.
The PLC in turn must monitor the safety system in order to understand when it can and cannot
act.
Your PLC program must take this into account so that it can differentiate between not being
able to act because the safety system has decided it is not safe to cycle versus there
being something wrong with the machine which prevents it from operating.
A few basic safety devices.
Here are a few basic safety devices.
I will not attempt to be comprehensive.
Rather, I am just giving a few common examples so that you will understand the environment
in which the PLC can operate.
Emergency Stop Circuit. A basic element of nearly all industrial machines is some sort
of Emergency Stop Circuit. When the on button is pressed, a relay will close and hold itself
on. This will enable power to the machine, including the compressed air supply if there
is one. If the stop or e-stop button is pressed, the relay will open and remove energy from
the machine, rendering it safe. If the electrical power supply to the machine goes off, due
to, for example, the building losing electrical power, the emergency stop circuit will also
drop out or open and remain off until the start button is pressed again. Well, every
or nearly every machine will have an emergency stop circuit. It is often not sufficient on
its own. In other words, it is necessary, but not always sufficient.

With two hand control, the operator station will have two large buttons, which the operator
must press simultaneously and hold to enable the machine to operate.
With both hands on the buttons, you know where the operator's hands are.
The operator must remove both hands from the buttons in order to enable the circuit again.
If one button remains closed and the operator attempts to activate the machine again with
the other button that the safety circuit will detect this and refuse to enable the machine
again until both buttons are deactivated.
This is the anti-tie-down feature.
The operator cannot tie one button down and cycle the machine repeatedly with just the other
button.
The buttons will be connected to a special relay which monitors and self-tests to ensure
it operates correctly.
The PLC will monitor an auxiliary contact on this relay so that it knows when to start
its sequence of operation, but the redundant safety contacts on the relay lie in between
the PLC and whatever hazards are being guarded against.
The safety device has ultimate control over whether the machine moves or not.
light curtain. Another basic safety device is the light curtain. This has a series of
closely spaced light beams across the opening which forms the operator's access to the
working area of the machine. If one of these light beams is interrupted, the light curtain
controller will not permit the machine to move. Light curtains can usually be used in
places where two hand control systems can be used. They have an advantage over two hand control
in that the operator can be performing other tasks while the machine is cycling instead
of being occupied with holding the two hand control buttons down. This allows for productivity
improvements which can usually more than pay for the higher cost of the light curtain compared
to simple to hand control.
Other devices.
There are many other safety devices, many of which address niche applications.
I won't bother listing any more than I have so far, however, as you should understand
the basic principles by now.
Safety PLCs.
There are special safety PLCs which have redundant CPUs which monitor one another and which have
redundant, mutually interlocked I.O. and which runs safety reviewed software.
Anything connected to a safety PLC must itself be safety rated if it could affect
the safety of the machine. However, these are quite rare and only used in
certain special industries. These are normally used in places where some
programmed sequence of operations is required to render a system safe. This is
more commonly found in places such as oil refineries, chemical plants, or electric power
generating plants than in typical factories.
Safety and Cybersecurity
This is a good place to bring up the question of safety and cybersecurity.
There have been a number of articles in the IT press recently about how PLCs could be
indirectly affected by computer viruses and how this could cause dangerous safety problems
in manufacturing equipment.
The premise is that they found security holes in software which runs on personal computers
running Windows operating systems which are used to do things like record production data.
There are a number of software systems which are designed for this purpose although SCADA
systems are usually the ones mentioned.
I will briefly describe SCADA systems in a later episode.
For our purposes here, however, just understand it as specialized industrial software that
runs on a PC and conducts monitoring and display using data from a PLC that it is networked
to.
According to these security researchers, a virus could exploit these security holes to send
and commands to the
PLC and cause it to do arbitrary things which could cause injury or death.
The PLCs being referred to in these instances are ordinary PLCs, not safety PLCs.
I find these claims to be highly implausible for reasons that I have stated above when
describing safety systems.
An ordinary PLC is not a safety device and so the safety of the machine should not be
affected by malfunctioning PLC regardless of whether any viruses were involved or not.
I have seen PLC's malfunction due to memory corruption errors, but these posed loss of
production problems, not safety problems.
A malfunctioning PLC may cause property damage to the machine and loss of money, but the
control system of which the PLC is only a part should not permit it to pose a hazard
to personnel. I have not seen any of these security researchers offer any plausible
mechanism by which their claims of safety problems may be realized. As a result of this,
I take all such claims with a very, very, very large grain of salt.
Conclusion In this episode, we look at the IO modules,
what they are, how they work, and the purpose that they serve in the system.
In addition to this, we discussed machine safety systems and also claims made by certain people
about cybersecurity and industrial safety.
In the next episode, I will cover networking, including a detailed look at one industrial
network protocol called Modbus.
This has been the fifth episode in an eight part series.
